ELI5: What's the advantage of Uber?

I started using Uber a year ago, then back to taxi a few times, then back to Uber. I actually find the Uber to be cheaper or the same price as a taxi, I don't have to tip, the car is a hell of a lot cleaner, and the driver isn't deliberately taking you on a foreign route to collect a bigger fare. If you have a problem with a driver, Uber Support will make it right.

Full Disclosure, I now drive Uber and Lyft on the weekends too. I joined up because of my many good experiences across the country with Uber as a passenger. Lyft, which doesn't have the market share, is a better experience for the drivers and passengers as Lyft does inspections of drivers and vehicles while Uber does not - also, Lyft seems to pay it's drivers better and has better liability insurance coverage.

It's generally cheaper than a taxi (in many cities--fares are about 30% lower in my city), and faster than a typical car service (because there are lots of Uber drivers, so you don't frequently need to pre-schedule a trip with them in advance).
Ah OK cool. The prices must have come down a lot.

I have friends/family in Chicago that I visit at least once per year, and I've used Uber almost exclusively while in town 2 trips (one in May, the other in November). I like the convenience of the app and have found it to usually be cheaper than a taxi both in the city and in the suburbs. Several times I found myself on side streets or areas that taxis didn't usually patrol looking for fares, but I can just push a button and an Uber comes to me. Also, I rarely have cash on me, so handling the transaction entirely on my phone is so much less of a hassle than using a credit card in a cab although I'm not sure if drivers everywhere get an attitude about cards or not, I've really only used taxis while in the Chicagoland area. As far as cost goes, I'd say I paid between 25-30% less for an Uber than I would have for a cab and like I said, it all happened on my phone so I wasn't worried about getting change or waiting for anything. Once I got to my destination I just thanked them and hopped out. I really didn't mean for that to sound like such a pitch, but it really is cheaper and more simple.

From my experience it's a lot better than taxis (specifically in Chicago). Also a tip, if you plan on going as a group with Uber, I don't think they accept more than 3, maybe 4 people in the car. With the 50% increase in fare due to high demand for Uber, it was ~ $6, when the same charge for a taxi was ~ $17 earlier in the day. So it is a lot cheaper.

The cost aside, I think there is a huge advantage for the driver from a perspective of security. Compared to regular taxi drivers, uber taxi drivers actually know who the hell is getting in their cars. Uber has all user's info, phone number, address, credit card info etc. before you get into any while as a passenger. Because of this very fact, I think Uber users, specifically passengers, are less like to commit any crimes towards the Uber drivers. Food for thought.

Galt house in Louisville to Buckslou was $7 plus tip by cab.

Uber on the ride back was $5, no tip allowed or needed.

Our Uber driver was great, allowed our upfront passenger to control the AC and radio, and his nearly new Maxima was about a hundred times nicer than any cab I've ever sat in, and it took about 2 minutes literally for him to arrive at the curb.

We went brewery hopping the next day, same deal, got great local recommendations from a driver our age, was cheap, fast and clean. I can't say that about any cab I've ever been in.

Don't forget to send invites to your friends for a free first ride, read the restrictions though, it's something like 90 days and up to $20, which should take you just about damn near anywhere in a city.

What We Learned: The case for Ryan O'Reilly's contract

We learned that a desperate rookie GM will give up a lot for a little and make mistakes that will hurt the team down the line. He's traded away 6 of our top prospects and dropped 3 high picks in the deepest draft in a decade. I have no doubt that the team is better now (that doesn't take much), but he didn't do it the right way. I believe the Sabres, and the league, are in a worse position for the future because of Tim Murray.

ROR is not worth that money, and now we have to balance that contract on top of Kane and Bogosian's when Eichel, Reinhart and our other prospects come looking to cash in in 2-3 years.

http://www.hockeybuzz.com/cap-central/team.php?team=BUF

We are still $15mil under the cap, with our major signings in place. ROR is the only one on the books for more than 3. We had a ton of room to play with, and if things continue the way they have for the NHL, the cap will grow. I have no problem with this contract.
I'm not so much worried about the cap as I am about setting a precedence about paying a guy almost Sidney Crosby money for putting up average points/year.

I'm not disagreeing on the precedent the contract sets and that it can likely have a negative impact on the league's cap situation as a whole. However, it is important to keep in mind that when Crosby signed that contract, it was about 17.3% of the cap (8.7/50.3) while ROR's is about 10.3% of the cap (7.5/73.0). For reference, a player signed to Crosby's '07 cap percentage today would have a cap hit of about $12.7mil.

While it is definitely an overpayment, I don't really see it as a desperation move. There is not significantly more pressure on Murray (from an outsider's view, maybe locally there is) to win next year. Part of that pressure, though, is likely him not wanting Eichel to marinade in a losing environment a la Edmonton and by that token, you got Eichel - don't waste even those first few years. Make the team competitive, if not a playoff team.

ROR is NOT worth that money at this very moment. And if Kane, Bogo, Eichel, Reinhardt, AND Ristolainen (I'm really hoping!) all require such significant raises when their contracts are up and it becomes a problem...its not the worst problem. One of them could be flipped for assets, though not close to what they gave up. Murray is definitely gambling that ROR will be worth it, but I think its optimistic that he sees that value (in relation to percentage of the cap) within the next three years. So, not desperate. But certainly not a sure thing ROR lives up to the contract.
Agree, I would be worried about the long term impact from this contract, especially when future Sabres want their extension and they use this contract as a baseline

Definitely. The contract has the potential to become an albatross in a few years for the Sabres. If he doesn't hit his potential, nobody is going to want to take on that contract with that term. Playing the risks and rewards is something every GM has to balance, but Murray seemed to go from a proper long term rebuild in taking time with prospects and picks to pushing for a quicker rebuild.

As Calzone said, moving 6 top prospects and flipping high draft picks looks bad now and will look worse if a couple of those develop. Fun fact, ROR will make as much as Steven Stamkos this season.

The article goes pretty well in depth on why its not that bad of a contract, I just think it's hard to swallow because it coincides with all the moves you mentioned like getting rid of high picks, prospects, ect. I don't think the contract is seriously outrageous, but couples with the other moves its questionable.

I think you're right, I'm definitely looking bigger picture here rather than each move as a separate event. It's a little hard for me to swallow seeing who were considered some of our best prospects traded away for one guy with a monster contract.
